Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a customer case study about a company that adopted a continuous delivery platform and now deploys more often. Around 250 words.

Northwind Freight shipped software twice a month. Every release meant a Friday afternoon meeting where three teams argued about whether the build was safe to ship, then a weekend where someone stayed near their laptop in case it wasn't.

The company switched to Harness's continuous delivery platform in January 2026. Engineers moved from manual sign-offs to automated pipelines: every merge to main triggers a build, a test suite, and a staged rollout that watches error rates before it continues. A bad deploy rolls back on its own within minutes.

The change in cadence was immediate. Northwind now deploys 40 times a week, up from twice a month. Lead time from commit to production dropped from eleven days to under four hours. The Friday meeting is gone.

"We used to treat every release like a controlled explosion," said Priya Raman, Northwind's VP of Engineering. "Now it's just Tuesday."

Smaller, more frequent deploys mean smaller diffs. Diffs that size get reviewed faster and conflict less often. Engineers report catching bugs within an hour of introducing them, rather than weeks later during a release cycle, because each change reaches production on its own instead of bundled with fifty others.

Not every metric moved the same direction. Northwind's on-call load rose in the first six weeks as the team tuned its rollback thresholds — the automated system flagged several false positives before engineers adjusted the error-rate window. By March, on-call pages had dropped below pre-migration levels.

Northwind will extend the same pipeline to its mobile release process next quarter. Mobile releases still go through app-store review and average once a month.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.
